==Problem==
Barb the baker has developed a new temperature scale for her bakery called the Breadus scale, which is a linear function of the Fahrenheit scale. Bread rises at <imath>110</imath> degrees Fahrenheit, which is <imath>0</imath> degrees on the Breadus scale. Bread is baked at <imath>350</imath> degrees Fahrenheit, which is <imath>100</imath> degrees on the Breadus scale. Bread is done when its internal temperature is <imath>200</imath> degrees Fahrenheit. What is this in degrees on the Breadus scale?

<imath>\textbf{(A) }33\qquad\textbf{(B) }34.5\qquad\textbf{(C) }36\qquad\textbf{(D) }37.5\qquad\textbf{(E) }39</imath>

==Solution 1 (Substitution)==

To solve this question, you can use <imath>f(x) = mx + b</imath> where the <imath>x</imath> is Fahrenheit and the <imath>y</imath> is Breadus. We have <imath>(110,0)</imath> and <imath>(350,100)</imath>. We want to find the value of <imath>y</imath> in <imath>(200,y)</imath> that falls on this line. The slope for these two points is <imath>\frac{5}{12}</imath>; <imath>y = \frac{5}{12}x + b</imath>. Solving for <imath>b</imath> using <imath>(110, 0)</imath>, <imath>\frac{550}{12} = -b</imath>. We get <imath>b = \frac{-275}{6}</imath>. Plugging in <imath>(200, y), \frac{1000}{12}-\frac{550}{12}=y</imath>. Simplifying, <imath>\frac{450}{12} = \boxed{\textbf{(D) }37.5}</imath>

~walmartbrian

==Solution 2 (Faster)==

Let <imath>^\circ B</imath> denote degrees Breadus. We notice that <imath>200^\circ F</imath> is <imath>90^\circ F</imath> degrees more than <imath>0^\circ B</imath>, and <imath>150^\circ F</imath> less than <imath>100^\circ B</imath>. This ratio is <imath>90:150=3:5</imath>; therefore, <imath>200^\circ F</imath> will be <imath>\dfrac3{3+5}=\dfrac38</imath> of the way from <imath>0</imath> to <imath>100</imath>, which is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }37.5}</imath> 

~Technodoggo

==Solution 3 (Intuitive)==

From <imath>110</imath> to <imath>350</imath> degrees Fahrenheit, the Breadus scale goes from <imath>1</imath> to <imath>100</imath>. <imath>110</imath> to <imath>350</imath> degrees is a span of <imath>240</imath>, and we can use this to determine how many Fahrenheit each Breadus unit is worth. <imath>240</imath> divided by <imath>100</imath> is <imath>2.4</imath>, so each Breadus unit is <imath>2.4</imath> Fahrenheit, starting at <imath>110</imath> Fahrenheit. For example, <imath>1</imath> degree on the Breadus scale is <imath>110 + 2.4</imath>, or <imath>112.4</imath> Fahrenheit. Using this information, we can figure out how many Breadus degrees <imath>200</imath> Fahrenheit is. <imath>200-110</imath> is <imath>90</imath>, so we divide <imath>90</imath> by <imath>2.4</imath> to find the answer, which is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }37.5}</imath>

~MercilessAnimations

==Solution 4==
We note that the range of F temperatures that <imath>0-100</imath> <imath>\text{Br}^\circ</imath> represents is <imath>350-110 = 240</imath> <imath>\text{F}^\circ</imath>.
<imath>200</imath> <imath>\text{F}^\circ</imath> is <imath>(200-110) = 90</imath> <imath>\text{F}^\circ</imath> along the way to getting to <imath>240</imath> <imath>\text{F}^\circ</imath>, the end of this range, or <imath>90/240 = 9/24 = 3/8 = 0.375</imath> of the way. Therefore if we switch to the Br scale, we are <imath>0.375</imath> of the way to <imath>100</imath> from <imath>0</imath>, or at <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) }37.5}</imath> <imath>\text{Br}^\circ</imath>.

~Dilip

==Solution 5==
We have the points <imath>(0, 110)</imath> and <imath>(100, 350)</imath>. We want to find <imath>(x, 200)</imath>. The equation of the line is <imath>y=\frac{12}{5}x+110</imath>. We use this to find <imath>x=\frac{75}{2}=37.5</imath>, or <imath>\boxed{D}</imath>.
~MC413551
==Solution 6 (extremely simple)==
We can write the value <imath>y</imath> on the Breadus scale as <imath>y = mt + b</imath>, where <imath>t</imath> is the temperature in Fahrenheit.
From the problem, <imath>110m + 1b = 0</imath> and <imath>350m + 1b = 100.</imath>
We can rewrite this problem in terms of linear algebra to solve it.

<imath>Let \: A =\begin{bmatrix}
110 & 1 \\
350 & 1
\end{bmatrix}, let \: B = \begin{bmatrix}
0 \\
100
\end{bmatrix}, and \: let \: x = \begin{bmatrix}
m \\
b
\end{bmatrix}.</imath>
We can write the system of equations as Ax = B.
We can solve for x using the expression x = <imath>A^{-1}B</imath>.
Calculating this value we get <imath>x = \begin{bmatrix}
-1/240 & 1/240 \\
35/24 & -11/24
\end{bmatrix}\cdot\begin{bmatrix}
0 \\
100
\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}
5/12 \\
-275/6
\end{bmatrix}.</imath>
Therefore, <imath>m = 5/12 \: and \: b = -275/6</imath>.
Plugging in <imath>t = 200</imath>, we get <imath>(5/12)200+(-275/6) = \boxed{\textbf{(D) }37.5}</imath>.

~Loquacious Autodidact
